title: HAI Seminar: The World Model and Spatial Intelligence Era: Governing AI Beyond Language
summary:
AI policy was built for systems that talk. What happens when AI can also see, navigate, and act in the physical world, and governance frameworks can't keep up?

World models are AI systems that build and maintain working representations of real environments, predicting how conditions change in response to action. They could transform infrastructure planning, crisis response, scientific experimentation, and embodied AI. They also raise governance challenges that language-focused policy was not designed to handle.

Building on a recent Stanford HAI Policy Brief, this seminar examined both the promise of world models and the gaps in current governance approaches.

This video was recorded at Stanford University on September 30, 2026.

title: HAI Seminar: Industry Conversation with Instacart
summary:
What does AI adoption actually look like inside a firm — and what happens to the people working in it?

This HAI seminar pairs two perspectives on that question. Alexandr Lenk of Instacart Economics will share findings on how AI adoption diffuses through peer networks inside firms and drives productivity gains, drawing on evidence from engineering and data-science teams. Arvind Karunakaran of Stanford MS&E will offer an organizational lens on what follows: how AI tools reshape roles, workflows, expert authority, and oversight relationships at work.

Discussion will explore where these two pictures meet, where they diverge, and how to assess the enterprise value of AI.

This video was recorded at Stanford University on September 23, 2026.

title: Rob Reich, Diyi Yang, Surya Ganguli | Prompt Response: Should AI Slow Down?
summary:
This discussion takes on the argument running underneath most current AI policy debates: whether the technology poses a genuine risk to humanity, and whether its pace of development can or should slow. Rob Reich (Stanford Political Science, HAI) brings a political philosopher's account of how societies govern frontier science, and why leaving the critical decisions to researchers who answer to corporate leadership is a pattern with a poor track record. Diyi Yang (Stanford Computer Science, HAI) brings the view from inside the systems themselves, where her group's research on AI agents in the workplace and on model failures across dialects and cultures documents harms already measurable today. And Surya Ganguli (Stanford Applied Physics, HAI) brings a technical perspective on how advanced AI systems learn and what their capabilities and limitations reveal about emerging risks. HAI Executive Director Russell Wald moderates.

This event took place on September 21, 2026.

title: People of ACM: Altigran Soares da Silva (10/06/2026)
summary:
Altigran Soares da Silva is a Professor at the Institute of Computing of the Federal University of Amazonas, Brazil. His research interests include data science, data management, information retrieval, data mining, machine learning, and large language models.

He has authored or co-authored more than 170 scientific publications and co-founded three technology companies: Akwan, acquired by Google in 2005; Neemu, acquired by Linx in 2015; and Teewa, acquired by Jusbrasil in 2019. He has served on program committees for numerous international conferences and workshops and was Editor-in-Chief of the Journal of the Brazilian Computer Society.

A member of the Brazilian Academy of Sciences, he also serves as the Latin America and Caribbean Regional Committee Chair of the ACM Global Engagement Board. The Board works to expand ACM’s global reach and strengthen computing communities around the world.

Read the interview at: https://www.acm.org/articles/people-of-acm/2026/altigran-soares-da-silva.

ABSTRACT

This AMA (“Ask Me Anything”)-style talk with Oana Olteanu will focus on what becomes possible when the primitives change: new interfaces, new abstractions, AI, software infrastructure, and especially the strange or unfinished things people are building before they have obvious categories.

We recommend these pre-reads before attending the talk:

Against Usefulness (https://www.motivenotes.ai/p/against-usefulness)
What I Learned at the First Conference Built for Agentic AI (https://www.motivenotes.ai/p/what-i-learned-at-the-first-conference)

Since AMAs are driven by questions from the audience, here are a few prompts that may help frame your questions for Oana:

-What has recently become technically possible that still lacks the right interface or abstraction?
-What are you building or experimenting with that doesn't quite have a category yet?
-What assumption about how software works do you think we no longer need to make?
-What are you seeing in your own field that feels important but isn't yet obvious?

title: Why Journal Editors Reject Your Research Paper Before Peer Review
summary:
Why do journal editors reject research papers before peer review? Learn how to address common causes of desk rejection, strengthen your academic writing, and prepare your manuscript for journal submission.

In this SciSpace webinar, an editor-in-chief explains how manuscripts are screened and what makes a paper worth sending for review. Drawing on examples from submissions he has assessed, the speaker examines unclear abstracts, weak research contributions, incomplete methods, unsupported conclusions, and referencing problems.

The session takes you through the research paper from title and abstract to results, discussion, cover letter, and submission. It also explains how to respond to reviewer comments and approach your next submission after rejection.

What you will learn

Choose the right journal and demonstrate fit: Check the aims and scope, audience, article types, author guidelines, and recent publications before submitting.

Strengthen your research paper: Write an accurate title and clear abstract, explain the research gap, report reproducible methods, and present results and discussion without overstating your findings.

Check reporting and research integrity: Understand the role of PRISMA, CONSORT, STROBE, and IMRAD, alongside reference verification, ethical approvals, authorship, and AI-use disclosure.

Prepare for submission and revision: Review submission files, write a focused cover letter, respond to reviewers point by point, and plan alternative journals when a paper is rejected.

The webinar also examines why sophisticated statistical analyses and impressive diagrams are not enough when the research question or scientific contribution is weak.

For PhD students, early-career researchers, faculty members, and academic authors preparing a research paper for publication.

title: AI in Academic Writing: Red Flags Journal Reviewers Notice | SciSpace
summary:
Using AI for academic writing or literature reviews? Learn which mistakes raise red flags in peer review and how to check citations, assess AI-generated text, and review your manuscript before submission.

This SciSpace webinar takes a journal and grant reviewer’s perspective on AI in research. The session moves from examples of careless AI use to practical demonstrations of literature searching, source verification, manuscript checking, and document editing.

What you’ll learn:

Recognize AI-related writing mistakes: Examine copied chatbot responses, fabricated references, incorrect DOIs, vague language, and statements that do not match the research evidence.

Verify sources and understand the literature: Follow a SciSpace literature review example, open original sources, check DOI links, and use Chat with PDF to explore passages, graphs, tables, and mathematical content.

Check and revise your manuscript: See an example of reference verification and citation-coverage checks, then explore changing references from APA to Vancouver in a research document with tracked changes.

The webinar also discusses AI disclosure, confidentiality in peer review, institutional and journal policies, algorithmic bias, and the speaker’s concerns about AI detectors. Throughout, the emphasis is on preserving your research voice, checking AI-generated output, and retaining intellectual ownership of your work.

For PhD students, researchers, faculty members, and academic writers who want to use AI to improve research quality—not simply produce more text.

title: How to Find the Right Journal & Get Your Research Noticed | Complete Tutorial | SciSpace
summary:
Learn how to find the right journal for your research paper, prepare your manuscript for submission, and promote your published work using SciSpace AI.

In this practical webinar, Dr. Joanne Donoghue demonstrates a research publication workflow that connects journal selection, manuscript formatting, and research visibility. Follow examples of turning an abstract into a journal shortlist, reviewing submission requirements, and creating content to share your findings with the right audience.

What you’ll learn:

Find a suitable journal: Compare journals by scope, audience, study type, indexing, publication fees, open access options, word limits, and decision timelines. Build a shortlist with backup choices and cross-check recommendations using publisher journal finders.

Prepare your manuscript for submission: Use journal templates to format an existing manuscript and its references, then review AI-generated feedback to identify areas that need your attention.

Build your research profile: Explore ORCID, Google Scholar, ResearchGate, and Web of Science, alongside the session’s explanation of h-index and Altmetric measures.

Promote your published research: Develop a publication promotion plan, identify relevant conferences and online communities, generate LinkedIn and X posts, and create a graphical slide deck highlighting your study’s design and findings.

The session also discusses reference verification, AI-use disclosure, and checking journal requirements before submission. The focus is on supporting your own research and publication workflow, not asking AI to write the paper for you.
